title: Wei Yi, Arjun, Rapport Win Again In Round 2 Of European Club Cup
summary: The favorites continued to cruise in round two of the 2026 European Chess Club Cup, with GMs Wei Yi, Arjun Erigaisi, and Richard Rapport among the stars to move to 2/2. Top seed Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club again rested GMs Anish Giri and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, which almost came back to bite when their leader GM Amin Tabatabaei lost to GM Temur Kuybokarov on top board. GM Volodar Murzin also looked set to lose, but pulled off an incredible swindle in a lost position to beat Marko Ivanovic and give the team a 5-1 victory. The European Women's Chess Club Cup already saw major clashes, with Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo overcoming fifth seed Odlar Yurdu with big wins for IM Stavroula Tsolakidou and GM Koneru Humpy. Third seed SuperChess Romania escaped with a 2-2 tie against eighth seed Club Ajedrez Linares, with WFM Viviana Galvan at one point missing mate-in-three in a crazy finish to a 121-move draw against IM Deimante Daulyte-Cornette. Round three is on Monday, October 19, starting at 8 a.m. ET / 14:00 CEST / 5:30 p.m. IST. There were still mismatches wherever you looked in round two of the Open, with none of the top-12 matches decided by less than a two-point margin. In fact, you had to go to the 17th table—just off the boards transmitted live—to find the first match upset. Dutch 17th seed LSG, led by GM Jan Smeets, slipped to a 2.5-3.5 loss to Danish 45th seed Hillerod Skakklub, led by GM Sune Berg Hansen. That didn't mean there wasn't a lot to enjoy, however, including impressive wins for some of the top players. Wei scored a sparkling win over IM Hilmir Freyr Heimisson to set Alkaloid on the path to a 6-0 victory over Icelandic team Breidabrik Chess Club A-Team. 17.f5? was a mistake in a promising position for White, while after 17...Nb4! 18.Rg1? Wei was able to pounce with a killer blow.

title: Wesley So Extends Lead; Status Quo In Women's
summary: After his three wins in the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship so far in different endgames, GM Wesley So defeated one of his nearest pursuers, GM Andy Woodward, in a pawn endgame in the eighth round. He is now on six points and extends his sole lead to a full point over GM Fabiano Caruana, to set up an all-important clash in the ninth round on Monday, after a rest day. Woodward, GM Jeffery Xiong, GM Awonder Liang, and GM Grigoriy Oparin, are all in the next point group with 4.5 points. IM Alice Lee missed a chance to capture the sole lead in the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship when she could not capitalize on a large advantage in a heavy-piece endgame against IM Anna Zatonskih. Lee continues to lead the table along with WIM Rachael Li on six points. In turn, GM Irina Krush could not make use of the opportunity and even lost to WGM Jennifer Yu to remain on five points. WGM Thalia Cervantes is in close pursuit of the leaders with 5.5 points after defeating the defending champion, IM Carissa Yip, with the black pieces. After a rest day, round nine resumes on Monday, October 19, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 8: Open Standings After Round 8: Women Round 8 Results: Open Considering that he had captured the sole lead at the end of the previous round, it was no surprise that So had increased his chance of winning the tournament. Still, there were always chances for the pursuing group to catch up with the leader, with successful results in the final stretch and the leader himself losing his grip on the proceedings. But, as it turned out, it was not to be. To start with, perhaps unhappy with the quality of his previous game and looking forward to rejuvenating on the rest day before the final three games, Liang made a quick draw with GM Abhimanyu Mishra. Caruana, too, could not make much headway with the black pieces against GM Sam Sevian and the game ended in a draw in 42 moves. Interestingly, Xiong's game against GM Ray Robson followed the same moves as So's game against Woodward until the 17th move, and Xiong seemed to have developed much better chances to press for an advantage than So.

title: Total Chess proposes unified rating system
summary:
Total Chess has proposed a new rating system that combines players' classical, rapid and blitz ratings into a single figure. Developed by researcher Mehmet Mars Seven in collaboration with Norway Chess, the formula uses existing FIDE ratings to assess overall playing strength across the three formats. Magnus Carlsen (pictured) tops the inaugural ranking, followed by Hikaru Nakamura and Nodirbek Abdusattorov. The system will undergo testing and public consultation before potential revisions. | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

One rating for three time controls

The Total Chess World Championship Tour has presented a proposal for a new rating system that combines players' classical, rapid and blitz ratings into a single figure. Announced on 14 October, the Total Chess Rating is intended to provide a measure of overall playing strength across the three main time controls. The system will initially be tested as a pilot, with the organisers inviting public feedback ahead of the Total Chess event scheduled to take place in Budapest from 10 to 21 November.

The proposal was developed by Dr Mehmet Mars Seven, a researcher at King's College London, in collaboration with Norway Chess. According to Seven, the original idea came from Norway Chess CEO Kjell Madland, who wanted a straightforward way to compare players' abilities across different formats. The system uses existing FIDE ratings as its starting point and produces a new figure on the familiar Elo scale.

Importantly, the Total Chess Rating is independent of FIDE's official rating lists and will not alter players' classical, rapid or blitz ratings. FIDE has agreed to observe the system during its pilot phase, following discussions within a working group involving the international federation and Norway Chess.

Norway Chess has been recently named "Best Tournament (Round Robin)" at the first FIDE Excellence Awards | Photo: Total Chess

How the new rating works

The new system combines a player's three FIDE ratings using a mathematical formula rather than calculating their simple arithmetic average. The distinction is based on the logarithmic nature of Elo ratings, in which a fixed difference between two ratings corresponds to a particular expected result.

The proposed method converts each of the three ratings into a measure of playing strength, calculates the average of those three values and then converts the result back into an Elo rating. The three formats receive equal weight, although the nonlinear conversion means that stronger individual ratings can have a greater influence on the final figure.

For example, Magnus Carlsen's ratings on 1 October were 2823 in classical, 2801 in rapid and 2860 in blitz. Their arithmetic average is 2828, while the proposed formula produces a Total Chess Rating of 2830.

The resulting figures retain the usual interpretation of Elo differences. A player rated 2800 would have an expected score of approximately 64% against an opponent rated 2700. This does not mean that the higher-rated player would win 64% of their games, since the calculation also accounts for draws.

The organisers argue that the formula provides a consistent overall ranking while approximately reproducing the results expected when games are distributed equally across the three formats. The mathematical reasoning, including the formula and its underlying assumptions, is explained in the full methodology published by Total Chess .

Carlsen tops the inaugural ranking

Total Chess has published an initial ranking of 100 players based on their FIDE ratings as of 1 October 2026. Carlsen heads the list with 2830 points, followed by Hikaru Nakamura on 2779 and Nodirbek Abdusattorov on 2774.

Alireza Firouzja occupies fourth place with 2765, while Javokhir Sindarov completes the top five on 2753. Arjun Erigaisi, Ian Nepomniachtchi, Wesley So, Fabiano Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu round out the top ten.

The complete top-100 ranking is available on the official Total Chess website.

Part of the new Total Chess championship

The rating proposal accompanies the introduction of the Total Chess World Championship Tour, a competition developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE. The project was announced earlier this year, with Norwegian footballer Erling Haaland joining as a strategic investor in Norway Chess through Chess Mates, a company established with businessman Morten Borge.

The new tour aims to determine a FIDE World Combined Champion through competitions featuring three formats: fast classic, rapid and blitz. The inaugural full season is scheduled for 2027 and is expected to feature four tournaments in different cities.

Before that, a pilot event will be held in Budapest in November, featuring 24 players. The field includes Carlsen, Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, Abdusattorov, Firouzja and Praggnanandhaa, among others.

The competition will begin with four groups of six players, who will contest double round-robin tournaments using the fast classic time control of 45 minutes plus 30 seconds per move. The knockout stage will combine four blitz games, two rapid games and one Fast Classic game per match, with a weighted scoring system.

Games played under the fast classic format will count towards participants' official FIDE classical ratings, and consequently will also affect the classical component used in calculating their Total Chess Rating.

Public consultation until December

Total Chess has invited players, organisers, mathematicians and chess followers to comment on the proposed rating system. Feedback submitted by 6 November can be considered ahead of the Budapest pilot, while the broader consultation will remain open until 24 December 2026 .

The organisers intend to discuss the methodology with players, FIDE representatives and other stakeholders during the Budapest event. Following the pilot and consultation period, Total Chess plans to publish the results of the review, including any significant modifications to the calculation method, in early 2027.

Comments and suggestions can be sent to Dr Mehmet Mars Seven at mehmet.mars.seven@kcl.ac.uk , with a copy to info@totalchess.com .

title: US Championships: So wins again, now a full point ahead
summary:
Wesley So defeated Andy Woodward in round eight of the US Championship to extend his lead to a full point over Fabiano Caruana, who drew against Sam Sevian. The two will meet in Monday's ninth round. In the women's tournament, Alice Lee and Rachael Li remain tied for first place on 6/8, while Thalia Cervantes moved within half a point of the leaders by defeating four-time national champion Carissa Yip. | Photo: Lennart Ootes / Saint Louis Chess Club

Open: So beats Woodward

Wesley So strengthened his position at the top of the US Chess Championship by defeating Andy Woodward in round eight. The three-time national champion now has 6/8 points, a full point ahead of defending champion Fabiano Caruana, who drew against Sam Sevian. Woodward, Jeffery Xiong, Awonder Liang and Grigoriy Oparin share third place on 4½/8, with three rounds remaining.

So's victory over Woodward was the most relevant result of the day. Playing white against the 16-year-old, So gradually simplified the position until the players reached a pawn endgame that appeared objectively balanced. However, Woodward made an inaccurate king move, allowing So to improve his position and eventually create a passed pawn on the queenside.

Further imprecisions enabled So to convert his advantage, securing his fifth victory of the tournament. He remains the only unbeaten player in the open section.

So v. Woodward

Annotations by Martina Gerdts

This was a battle between ChessBase authors!

The game began with the Ragozin Variation of the Queen's Gambit Declined.

After move 18, Wesley So still had 1 hour and 25 minutes left on the clock. A fair amount of material had already been exchanged. The players soon transitioned from the middlegame into a pawn endgame.

After 33.Kc3 , it was already difficult for Black to find a way to keep the balance. Black still had 33...a6 available, after which care would be needed to prevent White from breaking through. White still needed a few moves to find a promising manoeuvre.

Instead of 36...Kc6 , ...h6 would once again have been the more appropriate move. After 37.h4 , ...h6 is no longer possible because b5 wins the endgame. After 37.h4 , Woodward played 37...Kd6 , and So replied with 38.c5! bxc5 39.b5! , creating a passed pawn. The new sole leader went on to grab the black pawns on the kingside and win the game.

Caruana was unable to keep pace with the leader. Playing black against Sevian, the five-time US champion failed to obtain significant winning chances, and the encounter ended drawn after 42 moves. The result left Caruana alone in second place. Following Sunday's rest day, the ninth round will feature a direct encounter between Caruana and So, with the defending champion playing white.

The other decisive game saw Sam Shankland defeat Hans Niemann with the white pieces. Shankland obtained the better prospects and eventually converted his advantage, securing his second victory of the tournament.

Xiong missed an opportunity to join Caruana in second place when he failed to convert a promising position against Ray Robson.

Xiong v. Robson

White has a clear edge with his active king and better pawn structure. However, Xiong failed to find the precise move order to increase his advantage. Here 42.f5? gives Black a key tempo to play 42...Nc6 , and after 43.Ne4+ Ke7 44.Nc3 Black has 44...Nb4 , defending the all-important d5-square.

Instead, if White starts with 42.Ne4+, he gets to create the threat against the weak pawn on b6 in time: 42...Ke7 43.fxe5 fxe5 44.Nc3 and there is no good way to deal with the threat of Nd5+, with a clear advantage.

In the game, Robson continued to defend accurately until escaping with a draw.

Oparin also had chances against Levon Aronian, but failed to find the strongest continuations. Both games ended drawn, as did Liang's encounter against Abhimanyu Mishra.

Jeffery Xiong | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Grigoriy Oparin | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Fabiano Caruana will play white against sole leader Wesley So in Monday's ninth round | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Round 8 results

Standings after round 8

All games

Women's: Li and Lee remain atop the standings, Cervantes beats Yip and is now in sole third place

Alice Lee and Rachael Li maintained their joint lead in the US Women's Championship after both drawing their eighth-round encounters. The two players now have 6/8 points, half a point ahead of Thalia Cervantes, who defeated Carissa Yip. Jennifer Yu and Nazi Paikidze also scored victories, while Irina Krush missed an opportunity to catch the leaders.

Lee faced Anna Zatonskih with the white pieces and obtained a favourable position from a Catalan Opening. She gradually increased the pressure and reached a heavy-piece endgame with a considerable advantage. However, the 17-year-old failed to find the most effective continuation, allowing Zatonskih to organise her defence and eventually secure a draw.

Li also had opportunities against Tatev Abrahamyan. Playing black, the 16-year-old encountered difficulties after allowing her opponent to establish control over important dark squares. Both players subsequently missed chances to obtain a more substantial advantage, and the encounter eventually ended drawn.

Alice Lee v. Anna Zatonskih | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Rachel Li | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Cervantes took advantage of the leaders' draws, as she got the better of Yip with the black pieces. Cervantes obtained a favourable position against the defending champion, whose position deteriorated further after several inaccuracies.

The game ended abruptly when Yip overlooked a direct checkmate threat.

Cervantes now stands just half a point behind Lee and Li.

Krush missed an opportunity to join the leaders when she lost to Jennifer Yu. The eight-time national champion had recovered from an opening-round defeat to reach 5/7, but suffered another setback on Saturday.

The longest and most complicated game of the round was played between Paikidze and Anna Sargsyan. Paikidze found herself in a clearly inferior position and sacrificed her queen in an attempt to generate counterplay. Although the sacrifice was objectively mistaken, Sargsyan subsequently made inaccuracies that allowed Paikidze to turn the tables and eventually create decisive mating threats.

Paikidze v. Sargsyan

Annotations by Martina Gerdts

Paikidze felt that she had her back against the wall in this game. She did not go down without a fight, however, and promptly sacrificed her queen for activity.

The engine is not impressed by this move and would recommend 37.Qg1 Rxe6 38.Qd1, allowing White to continue fighting with two pawns and a piece for a rook. With only 11 seconds left on the clock, Paikidze played 37.Qxf2 and worsened her position in time trouble.

As the game continued, she sought shelter for her king behind her knights and advanced her e-pawn together with one of the knights towards the promotion square and the black king.

By this point, Paikidze had already managed to generate activity. The black queen on a3 later had the opportunity to capture on a2 with check, but the king simply moved via d3 to e2. The knight on d2 proved to provide sufficient protection for the king.

After 54...Bg5 , intending to attack the knight twice in the near future, White found a nice combination: 55.Rf7+ Kh8? 56.Rf3 Qb2 , and suddenly White was even better!

Both of Black's moves, 55...Kh8 and 56...Qb2 , were played by Sargsyan after only 2 and 3 minutes respectively. She should have spent more time here. After the combination, White was able to improve the position of her already active pieces and threaten mate. Once she had managed to shelter her king from Black's checks, Sargsyan resigned.

There was mate-in-four on the board.

After 67...Qxd2, there would follow 68.Rxh7#. The black rook can still sacrifice itself on d7 via c7, and the queen can do the same on b3. After 67...Qh6, the pawn can run through and White then delivers mate. Black has no way left to escape the mating net.

title: The hour of the seconds
summary:
The World Championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov is approaching. The contest gets underway on 24 November in Cologny, near Geneva. Who will be helping the two contenders this time? Sindarov will be able to count on the assistance of his compatriot Abdusattorov, among others, as Abdusattorov himself recently revealed. | Poto: UzChess / Yoav Nis

A World Championship match will be held again this year. From 24 November to 12 December, defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju (20, India) and his challenger Javokhir Sindarov (21, Uzbekistan) will face each other in a 14-game match to determine the new world champion.

The World Championship match will take place in Geneva, more precisely in Cologny, a suburb of Geneva. The games will be played there at the Fondation Martin Bodmer. The prize fund is 2.5 million US dollars, provided by software company Salesforce as the main sponsor and Timur Turlov's Freedom Holding as co-sponsor .

Behind every world champion stands a strong team

The two young players will, of course, try to show their best chess. To make that possible, a team of helpers works in the background. It is the "hour of the seconds" ( Stunde der Sekundanten ), as Alexei Suetin once described his work for Tigran Petrosian.

When Gukesh played his World Championship match against Ding Liren two years ago, he was able to count on the support of his compatriot Viswanathan Anand. The former world champion had played several World Championship matches during his career and was able to share his wealth of experience with Gukesh. He knows how important a good team of seconds is for such a match. Anand himself was certainly not involved in Gukesh's concrete preparation, but he passed on some of his own former helpers to his successor.

Grzegorz Gajewski and Radoslaw Wojtaszek, among others, were part of Gukesh's team. Gajewski had been Anand's helper in more recent years. Wojtaszek assisted Anand in several World Championship matches. The two Polish grandmasters also brought the strong Jan-Krzysztof Duda into the team. In Germany in particular, Vincent Keymer's involvement attracted attention. During the match, Keymer was based in Spain together with Wojtaszek and Pentala Harikrishna and supported Gukesh remotely.

Gukesh Dommaraju | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Remote control

As is well known, the World Championship match between Gukesh and Ding took place in Singapore, and for successful work by the seconds during a match, it is not necessarily a disadvantage if at least some of them are in a completely different time zone. While the game is in progress, there is nothing to do and the helpers can go to sleep. And when the players themselves are sleeping after the game, the seconds can do their work during the daytime in their own time zone.

It is quite natural for a player to hire mainly compatriots as seconds for his team. In the legendary Spassky-Fischer match, for example, the best Soviet players were part of Spassky's team and several Americans were on Fischer's team, even though Fischer did not listen to his people at all when it came to chess matters.

Compatriots preferred

It therefore comes as no surprise that Javokhir Sindarov will be supported, among others, by Nodirbek Abdusattorov as a second. Abdusattorov recently revealed this in an Uzbek podcast. These days, however, almost nothing remains undiscovered. Sindarov himself had already revealed that he is also preparing for the match against Gukesh with his regular coach, the Ukrainian Roman Vidonyak . Mukhiddin Madaminov will also almost certainly be part of Sindarov's team. He already helped him during the successful Candidates Tournament.

In Gukesh's case, all that is known is that Grzegorz Gajewski will again be on board. It would not be surprising if several others from Gukesh's 2024 team will be also involved again.

There has always been a certain amount of secrecy surrounding seconds, because their names can offer clues about the openings being prepared. Before the Anand-Kramnik World Championship match in Bonn in 2008, Kramnik had housed his seconds in a hotel somewhere in Germany and prepared with them there. By chance, someone close to Anand saw the group having lunch and passed the names on to Anand. At the opening press conference in Bonn, Kramnik was then asked about his seconds. Kramnik gave a few names in an attempt to create a smokescreen. Anand was sitting next to him, listened to what Kramnik said and then remarked that he was surprised by those names. He had expected the following people instead: Anand then named the correct players.

Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Javokhir Sindarov on their way to victory for Uzbekistan at the recent Chess Olympiad in Samarkand | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Sindarov is the favourite

After winning the World Championship title, Gukesh fell into a slump in form. In November 2024, his Elo rating was 2794. Two years later, it is only 2710. The world champion is now only number 28 in the world rankings. By contrast, Javokhir Sindarov's trajectory is upwards. With an Elo rating of 2782, the Uzbek is number 4 in the world. With a convincing victory over Gukesh, Sindarov might be able to overtake Caruana and Nakamura and would then be number 2 behind Carlsen. The Norwegian former world champion will probably not be caught before he eventually announces his complete retirement.

Nodirbek Abdusattorov is not the only one who sees his compatriot as the favourite in this World Championship match. Abdusattorov assesses the chances at 80:20. Of their three direct encounters in classical chess, Sindarov has won two games, while one ended in a draw.

But who knows? Gukesh proved to be a very resilient opponent against Ding, and as the saying goes, the truth is on the board.

title: European Club Cup: Comfortable wins for the favourites
summary:
The European Club Cup began on Saturday in Budva, Montenegro, with 108 teams competing in the open section and 22 in the women's tournament. The leading clubs secured comfortable victories, although there were a couple of individual upsets. Defending champions SuperChess Romania and Monte-Carlo both started with wins, while Novy Bor's Nils Grandelius suffered a surprising defeat against Serbian CM Slobodan Filipovic. The women's competition saw seventh seeds Crvena Zvezda held to a draw. | Pictured: Alkaloid's Arjun Erigaisi | Photo: Mark Livshitz / ECU

Budva hosts seven rounds of intense competition

The 41 st European Chess Club Cup and the 30 th European Women's Chess Club Cup got underway on Saturday, 17 October, in Budva, Montenegro. The competitions have attracted a record 130 teams, with 108 participating in the open section and 22 in the women's event. Both tournaments follow a seven-round Swiss system, with six boards per match in the open and four in the women's competition. The final round is scheduled for Friday, 23 October.

Most of the leading teams began with comfortable victories, although there were several individual upsets. Some clubs rested their strongest players for the opening round, while others fielded their leading grandmasters from the outset.

Read the full preview

All technical information on Chess-Results: Open | Women's

Open: Leading teams secure convincing victories

Top seeds Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club of Türkiye began with a 6–0 victory over England's Blackthorne. The Turkish team, which includes Anish Giri, Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, Richard Rapport and Amin Tabatabaei, did not need to field Giri or Erdogmus to secure the maximum score.

North Macedonia's Alkaloid, the second seeds, also registered a 6–0 victory, defeating Sharks 4NCL of England. Wei Yi and Arjun Erigaisi both played and won their games in convincing fashion. Elektroprivreda likewise scored six individual victories against SK Rockaden's second team, while Hungary's Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai defeated Niksic by the same margin.

Defending champions SuperChess Romania, whose squad includes Nodirbek Abdusattorov, defeated Iceland's Akureyri Chess Club 5½–½. Abdusattorov was rested, while well-known coach and former elite player Ivan Sokolov conceded the team's only half-point when he drew with the considerably lower-rated Bogi Palsson.

Novy Bor Chess Club of the Czech Republic also won comfortably, defeating Luxembourg's Gambit Bonnevoie 5–1, but suffered the day's most notable individual upsets. Swedish grandmaster Nils Grandelius lost to 55-year-old Serbian candidate master Slobodan Filipovic, who was rated approximately 450 Elo points below his opponent. Experienced Czech grandmaster David Navara was among the winners for Novy Bor.

Elsewhere, Vugar Gashimov and Beer Sheva Chess Club recorded 6–0 victories, while Ashdod Chess Club defeated Gambiet Opwijk 5–1. Rishon LeZion A also made a successful start, beating Cercle des Echecs Dudelange 5½–½.

Women: Monte-Carlo overcome young English opponents

Defending champions Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo, the top seeds in the women's competition, defeated She Plays To Win Lionesses A of England by 3½–½. Despite the convincing final score, the English team provided considerable resistance, particularly on the first two boards.

Aleksandra Goryachkina, the highest-rated player in the women's competition, faced none other than 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan and obtained a difficult win on the top board. On board two, Anusha Subramanian secured a draw against experienced Swedish grandmaster Pia Cramling. The remaining two games went to Monte-Carlo, with Stavroula Tsolakidou and Elisabeth Paehtz defeating their young opponents.

The rating favourites and defending champions from Monte-Carlo ended up prevailing against the young English team | Photo: Mark Livshitz

Several other leading teams recorded maximum scores. Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica defeated Klub Kolner Schachfreunde 4–0, while SuperChess Romania beat Gostivar by the same margin. Azerbaijan's Odlar Yurdu also collected all four points against Wasa SK, as did Gambit ASEE against SK Radnicki.

The most notable team result came in the meeting between 7 th seeds Crvena Zvezda and 18 th seeds Velikova Chess Club, which finished in a 2–2 draw. Meanwhile, Club Ajedrez Linares defeated Oslo Schakselskap 3½–½, and CE Gambit Bonnevoie achieved the same result against Davit Jojua's Chess Club.

With only 22 teams competing in the women's tournament, the leading contenders will meet relatively early. Monte-Carlo will face fifth seeds Odlar Yurdu in Sunday's second round, when Humpy Koneru is likely to make her first appearance for the defending champions.

The second round of both competitions takes place on Sunday, 18 October, starting at 14.00 local time.
